Asian Diesel Price Surge: Why the Philippines Felt the Pain Most in March 2026

In March 2026, diesel prices across Asia rose sharply due to Middle East tensions, supply disruptions, and currency pressures. But the Philippines stood out with one of the steepest increases in the region. Here’s a clear breakdown of what happened, why the Philippines was hit hardest, and how it compares to other Asian countries.

(See attached table for the full January vs. March 22, 2026 price comparison in Philippine Pesos per liter across the listed countries.)

Why the Philippines experienced the biggest jump

• Full deregulation under Republic Act 8479 (1998 Downstream Oil Industry Deregulation Act)  
  Prices are set purely by the market. Oil companies pass on global increases immediately with no government cap, subsidy, or delay.

• Weak Philippine peso  
  The exchange rate hovered around ₱59.8–60.1 per USD in March 2026, making imported fuel much more expensive in local currency.

• No consumer buffer mechanisms: Unlike most neighbors, the Philippines has no fuel stabilization fund, price freeze authority, or widespread subsidies at the pump during global spikes.

How other Asian countries limited the damage (comparison)

• Malaysia  -  Strong government subsidies keep RON95 and diesel prices artificially low. The government absorbs much of the global increase through budget support.

• Indonesia - Expanded subsidies and direct price controls. The government uses budget allocations to prevent full pass-through to consumers.

• Thailand - Operates an Oil Fuel Fund that subsidizes diesel, LPG, and other fuels during spikes. Temporary price freezes are sometimes applied.

• Vietnam - Uses a price stabilization fund, tariff waivers, and strategic reserve releases to smooth out sharp increases.

• Cambodia and Laos - Maintain more direct government controls and partial subsidies, especially on essential fuels.

• Singapore - No subsidies (market-driven like the Philippines), but starts from a much higher base price and has no equivalent deregulation “shock” because taxes and costs are already high and stable.

• India, Japan, South Korea - Mix of market pricing + strategic petroleum reserves, targeted subsidies for vulnerable sectors, and occasional government interventions to cap extreme spikes.

Political Context: Leadership Under Fire

Amid the fuel crisis, critics describe President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. as a weak leader whose administration appears more focused on political vendettas than on addressing the economic pain of ordinary Filipinos.

• Ongoing impeachment drive against Vice President Sara Duterte: 
 
  As diesel prices skyrocketed in March 2026, the House of Representatives continued pushing two active impeachment complaints against VP Sara Duterte (deemed sufficient in substance on March 4, 2026). Many see this as the President’s priority, diverting attention and political capital away from urgent issues like fuel relief and inflation control.

• Flood control corruption scandal:

  A massive graft scandal involving billions of pesos in flood-control projects (estimates of ₱42–118 billion lost annually) continues to rock the government. Despite public outrage and protests, the scandal has led to budget realignments and investigations, further eroding trust in the administration’s ability to manage national priorities effectively.

• “Shanghaing” of former President Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague: 

  The arrest and transfer of Rodrigo Duterte to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague in March 2025 — with confirmation-of-charges hearings held in February 2026 and Duterte still detained — has deeply polarized the country. Supporters view it as political revenge that shattered the once-united Marcos-Duterte alliance, weakening national unity at a time when strong leadership is desperately needed to tackle economic crises like the diesel price surge.

Bottom line:

The March 2026 diesel surge was a regional phenomenon driven by global events. However, the Philippines felt the full force because of its unique policy setup: complete deregulation combined with a weak currency and no automatic safety nets. Most other Asian countries in the comparison used subsidies, stabilization funds, or direct controls to cushion consumers — mechanisms the Philippines does not have under current law.

This structural difference explains why the percentage increase in the Philippines was significantly higher than in Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, and others — even though everyone faced the same global headwinds. Compounding the economic hardship is the political turmoil described above, which many Filipinos believe has left the country without focused leadership when it needs it most.

(Attach the comparison table image here for the full visual breakdown.)
#FuelCrisis #Philippines #AsiaFuelPrices

In Sept 2022, when NO other doctor dared 🔥, I organized & led a press conference/rally on the California Capitol steps against AB 2098—the bill branding COVID “misinformation” as unprofessional conduct, threatening license revocation for defying “scientific consensus.” 🩺🚫

Newsom called it a “witch hunt” for doctors... then signed it himself 😡. He knew: silence physicians, control patients. I stood up because the doctor-patient relationship was under siege. Spies in exam rooms? Forced propaganda on shots & mandates? UNACCEPTABLE. 🚨

Speakers included Dr. Len Saputo (50+ yrs licensed), Atty Leigh Dundas, Steve Kirsch & more. We warned: this destroys informed consent, violates 1st Amendment & Hippocratic Oath, sets precedent for ANY treatment (pain meds, chemo next?) ⚖️💉

Newsom signed anyway. 10 days later: first demand letter. Agents in black suits, guns holstered, tailed me to 5 locations. Manila envelope under my door—demanding patient charts without consent. 🕵️‍♂️

I refused. On June 5, 2023, live on The Adam King Show, I mailed my license & DEA number back to the Board 📬. Patients were prepped; I chose truth over compliance. 💪

I feel that targeting and retaliation cost me my CA medical license & Board Certifications in Anesthesiology & Critical Care (notified Dec 2024). No regrets. Zero. 🙅‍♀️

We spotlighted the tyranny—CA repealed AB 2098 in 2023 amid lawsuits & backlash. A stand for medical freedom, free speech, & patients’ right to full info. 🇺🇸🗣️

WAIT UNTIL THE END ⬇️ If they can silence your doctor, they can silence YOU. 

I fought for us all. ✊
#MedicalFreedom #AB2098 #NeverComply @DrMargaretShow

Right now, much of the conversation in the United States about the war with Iran is focused on rising gas and diesel prices, and what it’s going to cost us at the store. And yes, that matters.

But look beyond us.

Countries like the Philippines, which import the vast majority of their oil, much of it tied to the Strait of Hormuz, are being hit far harder. Fuel prices have surged to historic levels. Inflation is rising. The currency is weakening. Transport systems are under strain, and governments are being forced into emergency measures, even reducing work schedules to conserve energy.

And it’s not just the Philippines.

Across parts of Asia and Africa, nations that are not involved in this conflict are facing real disruption. This isn’t just about higher prices. It’s about whether transportation holds, whether food supply chains stay intact, whether daily life continues without breakdown.

We talk about inconvenience. Others are dealing with instability.

War does not stay where it starts.
